newsitem.title: USA: Grand Union debt off on restructuring news.
newsitem.headline: Grand Union debt off on restructuring news.

text.p: Debt of Grand Union Co whipsawed in early corporate trading as news the supermarket chain had initiated a corporate restructuring hit the market, high-yield traders said.
"The bonds traded off a few points to an 86-1/2 bid but have since come back to trade at 89 bid and are quoted a point off from yesterday's close," said one high-yield trader.

On Thursday, Grand Union said its restructuring would include 80 lay-offs at its Wayne, New Jersey, corporate headquarters and some division consolidations designed to save the struggling company more than $5 million.

"The reorganization was implemented to benefit all of our constituencies: customers, shareholders and the remaining 15,000 associates," said Roger Stangeland, board chairman and interim chief executive officer in a press release.

"This latest reorganization has further flattened and delayered our structure," Stangeland said. "In a very short time we have removed three layers of structure between the chief executive officer and the store manager so that only two layers remain."
The announcement coincided with the company reporting huge year-end and fourth quarter losses.

The company reported 1997 fourth quarter losses of $78.1 million versus losses of $29.3 million a year ago. Its fiscal 1997 year-end loss was $185.4 million versus an operating loss of $139.2 million in 1996.
While some players viewed the news as negative for the firm, others saw this as another positive step in Grand Union's attempt to move ahead in an extremely competitive environment.

"What this shows is that the preferred equity investors here, Shamrock and General Electric, are starting to really put their imprint on the company," said Dixon Yee, a high-yield analyst with Credit Suisse First Boston Corp.

Last July, the company announced plans to sell $100 million of preferred stock to fund 78 projects over the next three years, including new stores, replacement stores and enlarging existing locations.

On February 25, Grand Union sold $20 million worth of 8.5 percent Class A convertible preferred stock to an investment group which included affiliates of Shamrock Capital Advisors Inc. The investment group agreed to purchase a total of $100 million of these shares in stages by 1998.
Prior to that, $40 million was sold to Trefoil Capital Investors II LP, an investment vehicle for Roy E. Disney's family, and General Electric Co's GE Investments.

"This is reflected in the management changes we're seeing ... their CEO leaving a few weeks ago, their overhead reductions, and a possible acceleration of the drawdowns on remaining preferred equity investment that they agreed to last year," Yee said.
On May 7, Grand Union announced its president and chief executive officer Joseph McCaig resigned, citing differences with the board on how best to achieve the company's long-term objectives.

"We view that all as a positive. Unfortunately, the company still operates in a very competitive environment with extreme price competition, but I think they're taking the right steps in trying to rectify things," Yee said.
Meanwhile, on Thursday, Standard & Poor's cut Grand Union's senior unsecured debt rating to CCC from B-minus.

S&P cited the company's weaker-than-expected operating performance and cash flow protection measures for the last two quarters and concerns over the company's ability to reverse negative trends in the next year.
Grand Union's senior unscured debt is rated B3 by Moody's Investors Service Inc.
Grand Union operates 226 retail food stores in six Northeastern states.
(( -- Nancy Leinfuss, U.S. Corporate Bond Unit, 212-859-1675 ))
